 From shopping bags to stock charts 
 11:11 made me do it. 
From shopping bags to stock charts  
 Written by
 Claire Williamson 
 Financial writer
 Publication date 2026-11-13T05:57:14+0000 
 Start close to home with Shopee. For millions across Southeast Asia and Taiwan, the orange app is as routine as morning coffee. But traders aren't buying shopping bags – they're buying shares in its New York-listed parent, Sea Limited (NYSE: SE) .
 Timing is everything. Sea reported Q3 results on 10 November 2026, the day before 11.11. Group revenue climbed 43.4% year-on-year to US$8.58 billion and net income rose 34.0% to US$502.5 million. At Shopee, gross orders rose 25.5% to 4.5 billion, gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 23.3% to US$39.7 billion, revenue advanced 41.3% to US$6.07 billion and adjusted EBITDA rose 44.7% to US$269.2 million. Note that these figures cover July to September: they show Shopee's momentum going into 11.11, not how the sale itself will perform. 
 Shopee's core marketplace revenue – mainly transaction fees and advertising – grew 50.6% to US$4.60 billion, well ahead of GMV. That points to better monetisation (marketplace revenue over GMV is a rough indicator, not a pure take rate), and adjusted EBITDA growing faster than revenue is an encouraging sign for unit economics.
 Growth didn't ease every concern. Group-wide sales and marketing expenses rose 64.0% and the provision for credit losses jumped 82.3% – Sea-wide figures rather than Shopee-only, but costs investors must weigh against rising sales. Diluted GAAP earnings per share came in at US$0.78, and the board approved a further US$1 billion buyback, which may support sentiment but does not put a floor under the share price. 
 Here’s where traders get tripped up: GMV is not revenue, and a crowded virtual mall is not a guaranteed profit bonanza. When Shopee – alongside Alibaba’s Tmall/Taobao (BABA/9988.HK) , JD.com (JD/9618.HK) and PDD Holdings (NASDAQ: PDD) – unleashes vouchers, flash sales and live-stream subsidies, transaction volume spikes. But who pays for those discounts?
 If incentives, marketing and delivery subsidies erode the margin on each order, higher GMV won't impress for long. The real test is whether extra transactions convert into sustainable cash generation.
 Beyond the discount: Logistics and live-streaming
 Look past the headline numbers to how the sales are made. Two themes to watch:
 The logistics stress test: 11.11 puts fulfilment networks under heavy strain, and fuel, warehouse automation and last-mile delivery costs eat directly into margins. Smooth delivery at record volume signals strong infrastructure; bottlenecks send fulfilment costs higher.
 The live-streaming pivot: Shoppable video can lift engagement and impulse purchases, but creator commissions and paid promotion still need to earn their keep. Look for evidence of conversion and retention, not just views.
 From shopping bag to stock chart
 The earnings-day price reaction. Sea closed at US$77.96 on 9 November, up 2.94% for the session. After the Q3 release, the shares traded lower in pre-market – a reminder that strong revenue growth doesn't guarantee a rally when costs and earnings quality are in question. Pre-market moves are thin and can shift once the regular session opens. 
 Once 11.11 results start to land, comparing Sea, Alibaba, JD.com and PDD against a broad tech benchmark will help separate company-specific moves from sector sentiment. Three questions to ask:
 1. The expectation gap: Does 11.11 beat what the market expects, or is growth already priced in? Watch basket sizes and repeat purchases for real demand versus one-day bargain hunting.
 2. Promotional drag: Do vouchers and subsidies compress margins by more than the top-line gains, or do advertising and fulfilment efficiency protect profitability?
 3. Forward outlook: Do management's comments on Q4 demand, marketing spend and profitability change market expectations for the months ahead?
 What traders are watching next
 Beyond the sale itself, these catalysts could drive the next leg of retail price action:
 Alibaba, JD.com and PDD earnings and management updates: JD.com is due to report September-quarter results on 17 November, and Alibaba’s board meets on 18 November to approve its results. PDD has not yet confirmed its date, but ‘Earnings Whispers’ expects it to report on 23 November, before the US market open. Commentary on promotional margins, customer acquisition costs and monetisation will help separate a sector-wide trend from Sea-specific news. PDD is especially relevant given Temu’s push into Southeast Asia, so any update on Temu’s overseas spending or growth will bear directly on Shopee’s competitive position.
 Monthly US retail sales and consumer price index (CPI) prints: Risk appetite and the US dollar's direction shape foreign capital flows into APAC tech stocks.
 December logistics and fulfilment performance data: Delivery times and return rates across Southeast Asia and Greater China will show whether post-sale logistics costs dent fourth-quarter profitability.
 Year-end holiday guidance revisions: Any updates to full-year profit targets or inventory clearance through late November and December.
 The bottom line for traders
 The lesson of 11.11 is simple: Never confuse a busy checkout line with a booming balance sheet.
 Don't get swept up in the hype – watch the unit economics once the confetti settles. Whether you're eyeing ecommerce exposure or hedging against currency and macro shifts, trade the data, not the discount.
